findings.title: should_block? performs database writes during model validation
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and saves the record, and it is invoked from EmailValidator#validate_each, i.e. from inside User's validation chain. Validation must be side-effect free: UsersController#create calls user.valid? (line 168) and then user.save, so every signup attempt runs validation twice and match_count/last_match_at are incremented twice per attempt. Any other code path that calls valid? on a User (e.g. User#change_username calls valid?) also performs an unexpected UPDATE on the blocked_emails table during what should be a read-only check. The collected statistics are therefore inflated and unreliable, and writes occur at times no caller expects them. Move the counter update out of the query path (e.g. record the hit only when a signup is actually rejected, or use a separate logging step).

findings.title: Non-atomic match_count increment loses updates under concurrency
findings.body: should_block? does a read-modify-write: it loads the record, does record.match_count += 1 in Ruby, then record.save. Two concurrent requests for the same blocked email both read the same count and both write count+1, so one increment is silently lost. Since this counter is the mechanism for tracking how often a blocked email attempts to register, it will undercount. Use an atomic update such as BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now]).

findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, allowing trivial bypass
findings.body: should_block? looks up BlockedEmail.where(email: email) with an exact string match. The rest of the codebase normalizes emails (Email.downcase is used in UsersController#change_email and User.find_by_username_or_email), but nothing downcases the value here, and User#email is stored as submitted. A blocked address like 'spammer@example.com' can be re-used by signing up with 'Spammer@Example.com' or 'SPAMMER@example.com', defeating the entire blocklist feature. The lookup (and ideally the stored value) should compare downcased emails.

findings.title: Any server email error permanently marks the email invalid with a misleading message
findings.body: After a failed createAccount, the controller adds the email to rejectedEmails whenever the server response contains errors.email. This includes errors that are not about validity, such as 'Email has already been taken' or the whitelist/blacklist 'not allowed from that email provider' message. Once added, emailValidation shows the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') reason for that address with no way to distinguish causes, so a returning user who already has an account is told their email is simply invalid. Only add to rejectedEmails when the error is actually a blocked/invalid-email error (e.g. have the server send a distinguishable error code), or surface the server's real error message in the validation reason.

findings.title: No tests for the whitelist/blacklist logic moved into EmailValidator
findings.body: The EmailValidator spec only exercises the BlockedEmail branch, and it stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? entirely. The domain whitelist/blacklist logic (email_in_restriction_setting? and both setting branches) was moved verbatim from User#email_validator into this new class but has no direct tests here, and no integration test covers that creating a User with an email present in blocked_emails actually fails. There is also no test for the case-sensitivity behavior of the blocked lookup. The core behavior of this PR (blocked emails reject signups end-to-end) is untested.
